inline.s: There was a great famine in eastern Zhejiang. The throne appointed Master Zhu to the office of Ever-Normal Granaries Commissioner and other posts. As soon as he took up the charge, he sent letters to other commanderies, calling for rice merchants; he remitted their taxes. Day by day, with his subordinates, he searched out the hidden hardships of the people, until he forgot sleep and meals. Once his plans were settled, he inspected the territories under his charge, and there was no deep mountain or long valley he did not reach, comforting, inquiring, and relieving. Those he saved cannot be counted. Whenever he went out he rode in a single carriage and dismissed his attendants, and the least thing he required never fell as a burden on the prefectures and counties. Later, in a letter to the governor of Jianning, he said: The government of disaster relief differs from ordinary days; there is absolutely no principle by which one may bag game while sitting still with folded arms. The rich have much grain; let them keep back a fixed portion, to wait for the coming year, and obey the command of the officials in relieving the want of their neighbors. What is there that cannot be done? Persuade them by kindness and grace, charge them by the great principle of duty; those who do not comply, threaten with punishment; those who comply gladly, requite with reward. Why should one shrink from their resentment and anger, or fear that they will deceive one, and so do nothing? And again he instructed the counties under him, saying: Exhort the upper households; provide in brief some wine and fruit; invite them and urge them to contribute; make your courtesy generous; make clear to them where their advantage and harm lie. You must not let the clerks harass them. The upper households are rich and sufficient families, and will surely be able to understand this meaning; among them there may be those who cannot fully manage it, and you should again and again exhort them. Examine whether their means are real; measure out the increase or decrease. If they still practice deceit and resist, then record their names and report them, and wait for separate action to be taken. And again he said: Take few attendants with you; go in person to each place, one by one; you must not sit upright in some cool and comfortable spot, relying only on the township guarantors.
Master Zhu often said: If I incur guilt for saving the people, I would not presume to decline it.

Lu Jiaoshu of the Qing dynasty once said: We who hold the honor of a single appointment from the court have no way to repay it; only to love and nurture the common people, and so cultivate the primal vitality of the state, is our duty.

When Mister Lu first took office at Jiading, he established the method of voluntary payment deadlines for the collection of taxes. He had each person who owed payment set his own limit and pay a certain amount by it; when half was paid by the due date, the man was pardoned. For this reason he never once had need of the rod, and yet those who owed payment came in a rush. Only the hardened tax-dodgers and stubborn households were given the rod now and then. Seeing how many were paying, Mister Lu feared the people were borrowing money to do it, and at once issued a notice that they must wait for the later deadline.

On every second, fourth, sixth, and eighth day, when the business of the hall was finished, he went to the school to hear the students expound the texts. Any promising student of the Confucian classics was permitted to join the students and listen. Examination papers he marked with brief comments only, not ranking them as superior or inferior. The texts expounded must all be brought home to one's own person and mind; they were not to be undertaken merely as a means to official advancement. He also set a policy question each time, requiring the students to go home and investigate it until it was clear, wishing the learners to master statecraft as well.

In judging cases, Mister Lu did not bind himself wholly to the statutes. When hearing a case, words of filial piety, brotherly duty, loyalty, and good faith never left his lips, and with gentleness and compassion he moved them by utmost feeling. After a year and more at Jiading, litigation had grown exceedingly rare. Again, because local custom favored extravagance and idle pleasure-seeking, he sternly prohibited and corrected it, teaching and admonishing with earnestness, and took the lead himself in person; and so the custom was changed. Again, in the market towns there were bands of strong-armed brawlers who joined together and made themselves a misery to the neighborhood. Mister Lu made a thorough inventory of their names but did not arrest them at once. When someone lodged a complaint, he would reprimand the offender and fasten him in the cangue at the gate, admonishing and instructing him from time to time; and when he saw from the man's looks that he had truly repented, he released him. In less than a month the whole gang had scattered and become good subjects. He also composed a text to exhort the prisoners and sent clerks to the jail to read it aloud, at which all the prisoners wept aloud.

Mister Lu kept his integrity as pure as ice and loved the people as his own children. Because of an inadvertent error he was dismissed from office, and the whole populace mourned and grieved. Before he left, they shut the markets in alarm; after he left, every household made offerings to him.

He held office a second time as magistrate of Lingshou county. Fearing that the country folk were without understanding, he went through every village to expound the village lessons, so that everyone might know that good ought to be done. All the words he used in explaining matters to the common people he gathered into one volume and gave it to the printer. He once said: A paltry single volume, expounded twice a month on the first and fifteenth — could it really put an end to violence and do away with killing? It is enough only to make a beginning. As for broadening it and filling it out, drawing it forth and extending it, so that every household understands and every person knows, soaking into their very flesh and marrow, all that is foul and filthy washed clean, all dregs dissolved — that depends on how the work is carried on from this day forward.

As magistrate of Lingyi, he was assigned to transport the coal required for the imperial tribute, carried by mule carts, five carts' worth, more than any other county. Mister Lu was the first to petition against it, and contended even to the point of resigning or staying; only then was the quota changed and shifted elsewhere.

As magistrate of Lingyi, there was a man named Wang Kui who had sold himself into servitude under the banners. A bannerman bearing a letter from a man of power came to demand the sealed indenture, and to carry off Wang Kui's wife, née Xu, along with him. Mister Lu resolutely gave from his own salary to redeem her and bring her home.

Lingyi county lies against the hills and borders the river, and here and there were stretches that could be cultivated and harvested. The common people feared that as soon as they sowed and tilled a single strip, they would straightway be assessed for tax, and that what they took in would not suffice to complete the tax; the profit was limited while the harm was endless. So they warned one another and dared not break the ground. Mister Lu issued proclamations everywhere, saying: No magistrate, unless he were raving mad, would force you to register for tax and so leave you an endless harm. Thereafter people gradually began to open such land.

There was a great flood in Lingyi. Mister Lu went in person to every village to survey the damage and took every means to protect the people; he reported at once to his superiors and begged them to memorialize for remission of taxes. When the time came to relieve the famine, Mister Lu wrapped up his own rations and hurried about every day, reaching the deepest valleys, and in all forty-five days the work was done. Again, in Lingyi the harvest failed year after year, and Mister Lu relieved the people by every means, so that the whole populace was kept safe. At the time some were collecting money to put on theatricals; he sternly reprimanded the ringleaders and used what they had collected to help fund the gruel kitchen. Mister Lu was afterward summoned to the capital and made a censor; he was given the posthumous title Qingxian, Pure Offering, and was honored with sacrifice in the Confucian temple.

The Complete Works of the Two Cheng Brothers, and the great compendium of Master Zhu's collected writings and the great compendium of his classified sayings, contain extremely detailed records of governmental affairs. One whose heart is set on this world need only gather a single volume from them, and there is no administrative matter that will not have its model there. Even the recent chronological biography of Lu Qingxian also contains good government worthy of imitation. Here, because the present compilation is narrow, it is not made complete.

Master Yan Guangzhou, in his Discourse on Filial Piety and Fraternal Duty, says: Youzi said that filial piety and fraternal duty are the root of benevolence. Mencius said that the Way of Yao and Shun was filial piety and fraternal duty, and nothing more. This filial piety and fraternal duty has the vastest bearing: across and lengthwise, from antiquity to the present, without bound or border, it is all this one matter. Yet one must understand what filial piety and fraternal duty is, and from what root it springs. Man, between Heaven and Earth, is a single breath. Since the first coming of the cosmos, there has been no day without birth, and all is living and alive. Benevolence is life. When my hands and feet are alive, I feel pain and itch; where they are numb and paralyzed, I feel neither pain nor itch. Among the ten thousand things of Heaven and Earth, when I see those that move, those green and fresh, those that dance and leap, those that sigh and cry out, they stir my breast and there is life in them, and their pain and itch are bound up with mine. This is what is called benevolence. And where does the living part of my own body come from? It follows this vital essence, yet the vital essence is not my own; it follows this form and color, yet the form and color are not my own. Both were divided off from my two parents. Consider: in the mother's womb, when the mother breathes out I breathe out, when the mother breathes in I breathe in. What nourishes me is the mother's womb; what I feed on is the mother's blood. Was there any body of my own here? Once I leave the womb and come forth from her arms, only then do I have life. Yet where is it that I am not leaning upon my parents? Consider the little child: all day long awake, he is awake with his parents; all day long asleep, he is asleep with his parents; all day long laughing and smiling, crying and wailing, it is all laughter and crying with his parents. Set the parents aside and he can unfold not a single plan, cannot stand up a single feeling. Is there still a body of his own here? This is the life of one whole household. All the papas and mamas, elder brothers and elder sisters of the household play with the little child, and the child, wholly without east or west, leans on the papas and mamas, the elder brothers and elder sisters, and makes one piece with them. Which is your kindness, which is my resentment; which is your right, which is my wrong? Is this not a single undivided whole? This is what is called benevolence. Benevolence is man; it is originally the making of father and son, elder and younger brother into one person. Later, when he has grown a little, he no longer leans on his parents to walk or stand: of himself he has a mind to run and jump. He no longer leans on his parents for joy and anger: of himself he has a mind to play and to be stubborn and contrary. He no longer leans on his parents for food and rest: of himself he has a mind to fancy fine flavors and to seek his own advantage. Is not his own self showing itself more each day, and growing gradually apart from his parents? And the parents, for their part, do not see through this mechanism; they poke and prod him, only fearing that he will not enter into the ways of the world and will not form a self. In everything they praise him, saying: My good darling, my good darling. This stirs in him the root of praise and blame, the root of craving for what is outside. In days to come it becomes the temper that parades its own goodness, boasts of its labors, prizes reputation, and puts on a show of integrity. To his brothers they tease him, saying: This is my son; this is the false one. This one has my love; this one has not my love. This stirs in him the root of jealousy, the root of self and other. In days to come it becomes the temper that blocks the worthy, envies excellence, and refuses concord with his own flesh and blood.

Meeting with food, they tease him, saying: I want more, I want more. This stirs in him the root of the greedy mouth and the root of greed and covetousness. In days to come it becomes the temper that fights over fields and goods and takes bribes and squeezes out wealth. When he suffers some small loss or gain and cries in distress, they say to him: Who has provoked my son? I will beat him. This stirs in him the root of violence and the root of grudge and gratitude. In days to come it becomes the temper that betrays the common good and builds factions and secretly strikes and harms. Such tempers, opening and showing themselves more and more, in the end leave even the parents unable to keep their own son. Why? Because parents too cannot always speak kindly, cannot always be tender; food and things cannot always be supplied in full measure, and affection cannot be without its gains and losses. And so all that was once used to teach the son becomes a tool turned back against the parents. Between family members, father and son, there arises the sense that you are wrong and I am right. When a plan of his succeeds, he takes much credit for it; when it draws criticism, he says: This is just how my parents are. Within the rooms and chambers, within laughter and talk, gratitude and grudge, win and loss, cannot be told out. Thus the parties of Niu and Li, of Luo and Shuo, already exist inside the family; and the contests of bowing and yielding and of seizing by force are already divided within one hall. How much more when outside lures drive him on, when a wife's words dazzle and confuse him, when children and servants urge him on! Can one be called benevolent in such a state? And being so oneself, can one forget thing and self and make even the favorable and the contrary with others? Now and then there is one or two who understand principle and have some aspiration, who stubbornly resolve to be filial, stubbornly resolve to be a good younger brother. Yet since beginningless time the habit-mind and habit-energy are hard to level and hard to release. So by a hundred means he presses it down, and of a sudden the root of arrogance and sloth appears; by a hundred means he complies and defers, and of a sudden the root of rudeness and contrariness appears; by a hundred means he yields and gives way, and of a sudden the root of I-can, I-know appears. If this root is not penetrated through, then spirit and complexion will suddenly leak out. Father and son, brothers, are sure to have someone secretly spying out the subtle signs, and so they cannot be glad and happy, wholly without trouble. Therefore filial piety and fraternal duty is a thing without a husk. What has a husk can never be roused and stirred; what has no husk will reach throughout the world. Why? Because there is no self in it. It is patience under insult. It is gladly placing oneself low. It is giving others harmony without a word. When this is present in a family, the family is moved; when it is present in the world, the world is moved. Therefore, when a child in the east cries for its mother, when one in the west leans on his son, wherever one meets with filial piety and fraternal duty one must think how to comfort and console. When the old are without anyone to turn to, when the young are in distress, wherever one meets with filial piety and fraternal duty one must think how to provide for them to the end. For those on labor service and the soldiers on the frontier, who have no leisure to care for father and mother, wherever one meets with filial piety and fraternal duty one must think how to give them rest and relief. For the roe and the minnow, the unborn and the newly born, the bird tending its young and brooding its eggs, the grass in flower and the tree in leaf, all that clings to its root and leans on its sprout, wherever one meets with filial piety and fraternal duty one must think how to moisten them with the dew of mutual care and to keep them whole. When there are such living stirrings as these, truly, call on Heaven and Heaven answers; call on Earth and Earth responds; so that even among the wild tribes and alien kinds, none with blood and feeling is outside this connection. How then could there be any lack of benevolence?

I have observed the filial sons of old: with some, the fierce birds did not snatch and the fierce beasts did not seize; there appeared the auspicious star and the felicitous cloud, good omens and signs of blessing. Was this not brought about by their compliant virtue? Heaven and Earth move in accord with what is fitting, and so the sun and moon do not err and the four seasons do not deviate. The sage moves in accord with what is fitting, and so punishments are clear and the people submit. That atmosphere of one harmonious contentment, in which one offers rich sacrifice to the Lord on High and is benevolent toward Heaven and Earth, and in which one is dutiful toward one's ancestors and filial toward one's parents, is all in this. Beyond this, what other business is there? Mencius says: Yao and Shun — filial piety and fraternal duty, and nothing more. He also says: The Way of learning and inquiry is nothing other than seeking back the heart that has strayed, and nothing more. These two and-nothing-more fit together exceedingly well. If filial piety and fraternal duty could not include the seeking back of the strayed heart, and the seeking back of the strayed heart could not include filial piety and fraternal duty, then it would not be the one thing that settles a hundred matters at a stroke. For the heart is not a round hollow shell; it is originally gentle and glad, originally full of tender ache, originally abundantly alive. When the sky clears and the earth is bright, the eye and the heart both open; when sky and earth are dark, sorrow and confusion are silent — this is Heaven and Earth as one heart. When grass is tender and trees tall, when birds bathe and deer couch, there is boundless delight; when cliffs fall and walls collapse, when there is cruel wounding and early death, there is boundless desolation — this is the ten thousand things as one heart. To forsake this and crave advantages, to delight in calamity and rejoice in misfortune — that is what is called the strayed heart. And even if not that, a heart that seeks fame and hates ill repute, a heart that wants wide reading and much gleaning, a heart that prizes reputation and puts on a show of integrity, a heart that withers in silent guarding — that too is called the strayed heart. Why? Because it does not belong to the life of my own heart. Therefore it was said above and plainly: Benevolence is the human heart. Filial piety and fraternal duty are the first revelation of the root of benevolence, its first swelling and sprouting. If here the root is kept alive, then branches follow, leaves are strung, and a thousand flowers and ten thousand blossoms all break forth together. It is like a man's one body: the ear hears, the eye sees, the hand holds, the foot walks — which of these is not one mass of living growth? And the Daoists cultivate themselves only by refining the spirit and vital breath to purity and guarding the One, and of themselves they can attain long life and light ascent. For when one place is numinous, even the joints and bones are numinous. So it is with filial piety and fraternal duty toward Heaven and Earth, the people, and all things: it is likewise the spirit and vital breath of the whole body, the elixir-head of self-cultivation. When the elixir-head is taken in hand, to shed the ordinary and become a sage lies within a moment; there is no further work of adjusting the joints. Therefore I once turned a phrase for it and said: The Way of learning and inquiry is benevolence, and nothing more. The Way of benevolence is filial piety and fraternal duty, and nothing more. These two and-nothing-more fit close and exact, with no seam left behind.

He also says: The reason the world is disordered and unsettled is only a hardened heart and fierce temper, which swell into anger, clash into brute force, and rush madly into attack and war and pursuit. The troops of Zhuolu, the roaring of the seven mighty states, the war drums of Huangchi and Yuyang — look at what stirs the breath within them and overturns Heaven and Earth like a wave. What is it? At first it was only a little breath of perversity, lying crosswise in the breast; gradually it was provoked and rose up, and could not be swallowed down. And so one resists father and elder brother, and is insolent to those above one. The root of this resistance and insolence is what will lay hold of officials and elders; it is what will bury men alive and take revenge; it is what will gather bands of the disaffected. Therefore the Commentary on the Book of Changes says: In litigation there must surely be a rising of the multitude. It is not only litigation before officials and elders. When a man himself has a heart that parries right and wrong and contends for victory and defeat, the posture of stretching the bow and rampaging is already visible. Yao spoke to Danzhu, saying: Is it fitting to be clamorous and litigious? And Yu's admonition says: Do not be like Danzhu in arrogance. Trace the word litigation to its bottom, and it is only the one word arrogance. Therefore one who is arrogant in serving his parents can certainly not be filial; arrogant in serving his elders, he can certainly not be loyal; arrogant in governing the people, he can certainly not be benevolent. The single word arrogance makes a man a home for accumulated evil and worthlessness, and there is no saving him. Therefore the gentleman has a great Way, and it is surely through arrogance and extravagance that he loses it. The arrogant and extravagant man is haughty and overweening, honors himself and despises others, calls himself right and others wrong, thinks himself wise and others stupid. What mood has he left for reckoning the people's interests and ills or thinking on the people's hardships? The one book, the Great Learning, from regulating the family up to bringing peace to the world, is nothing but filial piety, fraternal duty, and parental kindness. So the arrogant and extravagant man is plainly unfilial, undutiful, and unkind. Yet although he is unfilial, undutiful, and unkind, in the end he is still not the same as others. Therefore though a man be of the firmest, he cannot but bow before his parents; though of the harshest, he cannot but yield before his elders. This is the heaven-given nature that cannot be dissolved. Consider an unfilial man: before others he too restrains and adorns himself a little. If you made him sit while his father stood, he would certainly be uneasy. If you called him filial he would be pleased; if you called him unfilial he would be angry. This too is the place where the human root is not yet cut through. This uncut place is where blood and feeling enter in, and it is where my transforming influence can find room. Therefore a filial son and a dutiful younger brother can be turned with a single touch. So it was with Duke Zhuang of Zheng, who put away his own mother: when Ying Kaoshu, eating meat, set some aside for his mother, what business was that of his? Yet at once he was utterly remorseful and awakened. So too with Zigao, who kept mourning for three years, weeping tears of blood, and never once showed his teeth: what had that to do with the administration of the Cheng steward? Yet it happened that a man's elder brother, on the point of death, wore mourning for him because of Zigao. Here one does not know what moves and what answers, what touches formlessly and turns the viscera within. This is precisely the unwrought Heaven, the uncontrived mandate present there. The elder Shi You and his brother quarreled over land; because he spoke with Yan Feng in a boat about the matter of the property, Feng wiped away tears without ceasing, and You was greatly awakened. Such matters as these are all past understanding. Master Yan was himself filial and fraternal; what business had he to meddle with the Shi family? Yet he wept tears that ran crosswise, and no one knows how each drop fell into Master Shi's belly.

Broadly speaking, between Heaven and Earth, those who have ambition and spirit, sharp corners, and calculation will all push others away. Those without root and without stalk, who can do nothing about it and are unaware of themselves, are the very ones who can move others. Even in the market streets, among the most foolish and the most lowly, if a filial son appears, everyone will either praise him aloud or reverence him, or else silently bear a secret shame before him. In that moment of reverencing him and being ashamed before him, truly the harsh heart is leveled and the restless heart released. It is a scene all tenderness held in the cupped hands, all compassion. In a family it makes the family level; in the world it makes the world level. Above, from officials and elders, up to the ruler and his ministers, the greater the power, the more the multitudes drawn by his breathing; how then could the whole world fail to be filial sons and dutiful younger brothers to him? Therefore it is said: When one family is benevolent, a whole state rises to benevolence. And again: Yao and Shun led the world by benevolence, and the people followed them. The mechanism lies precisely here. When the customs of the world are bad, they are mostly ruined first in a man's time as a son and younger brother; when character and mental arts are bad, they too are ruined first in youth. Let there be the slightest friction, and he cannot bear it; let there be the least talent and spirit, and he cannot take it in. So when he comes at last to manhood, he lets out every kind of outrage, and no one can withstand it. Since old times, the sweeping and the answering, the bearing of the armrest, the standing in attendance — all of it is meant to wear away the son's and younger brother's fierce ambition and hardened temper, and to make him pull inward to the subtlest point. So too with the son of the Son of Heaven, who took his place in the ranks and proclaimed his humility, saying: When the ruler is present, the rites are thus; when the father is present, the rites are thus; when the elder is present, the rites are thus. What meaning is here? The world need not fear the lack of talent and ability; it fears the lack of true nature. It need not fear the inability to be ruler, father, or teacher; it fears the inability to be a good son and younger brother. If you serve one in the manner of a son, everywhere there is the meaning of one who may be served and cherished. If you serve one in the manner of a younger brother, everywhere there is the meaning of yielding the field's edge in plowing and yielding the road in walking. In old times, when Shun and Yu possessed the world, the world was just then singing their praises, bringing lawsuits and cases, and coming to court to see them, in the height of their blaze of glory; yet Shun looked on himself as no more than a poor man of Yu. The well and the granary still stood; only he was not to be seen. He wailed in the fields, and just then hated that he had no one to whom to appeal — yet the world was already governed. Yu looked on himself as no more than the son of a criminal of Yushan; his father's pain could not be redeemed; the vast waves appalled his bones; and meeting a criminal on the road, he wept several rows of tears without knowing it — yet the world was again governed. So it was with the filial piety of Kings Wen and Wu; there is none of it that is not thus. Wen still went daily three times to the door of King Ji's chamber; he still concerned himself with every matter of his father's breath and presence, and everywhere received his guidance and commands. Therefore it is said: Serve the dead as you serve the living; serve the departed as you serve the present. For Wen and Wu did not end as rulers of men, but ended as sons of men. Picture how they cherished the widowed and the solitary and comforted the people and smote the violent, having in their breasts nothing but this mind of the men before them, bright and unshakeable. As for Danzhu's enlightenment, was he without talent? Yet the one word arrogance had already cut through and severed the root of the world's mandate. That is why the Five Constants and the Hundred Offices were entrusted to the man of the Youzeng clan.

He also says: When the sages speak of filial piety, it is never a small matter. The Book of Rites says: Small filial piety uses strength; middling filial piety uses toil; great filial piety is without want. When the Master spoke of the great filial piety of Shun, he straightway spoke of virtue making one a sage and great virtue receiving the mandate; plainly, it is completing what Heaven gave birth to, and serving one's parents with Heaven. One must understand what a parent is: not a parent of one lump of blood and flesh. And what is this I that was born of my parents? Not an I of one lump of blood and flesh. It was originally round and solid, bright and shining, everyone made into one piece. The parent is also this; Heaven and Earth and all things are also this. My parents gave birth to this one body of mine; then one must take all that the body has and offer it up entirely to one's parents — that is gathering compliance. If one only uses strength and uses toil, serving that coarse form and appearance, while the one point of empty numinosity, the true bone and blood, the boundless treasure, is cast aside and left unattended — can one be called a filial son? In serving my parents, again, I must take every limb and joint of my parents, every thought and movement, down to their tears and spittle, their stool and staff, and serve them with my whole devotion; yet if the one point of empty numinosity of my parents, the true bone and blood, the boundless treasure, is cast aside and left unattended — can one be called a filial son? Therefore, as soon as one speaks of great filial piety, it is complying with one's parents and nourishing their aspiration. To comply with one's parents is to comply with the numinously wondrous parent; it is to comply with the parent as yet undivided from the prior Heaven. The parent sunk in the midst of feeling and consciousness is a false parent. To nourish their aspiration is to nourish the aspiration of the great common good; it is to nourish the aspiration that pierces the earth and reaches Heaven and embraces the people and all things. The aspiration within the shell of the body is a false aspiration. Yet to comply with one's parents and nourish their aspiration, one must further make the self sincere and guard the self. To guard the self is to guard the self that understands goodness; it is to guard the self that uses great virtue to practice the great Way. Otherwise, even to exert all one's strength in care and support and to serve with a soft countenance is still a false self. Only one who can recognize the true self can begin to recognize the true parent. Therefore it is said: If one is not sincere in oneself, one does not comply with one's parents. The self of Zengzi and the self of Zeng Yuan were far apart; therefore what they served their parents with was likewise different. Now let us look at the filial piety of Shun and of Wang Xiang. Wang Xiang's filial piety was utterly true and utterly earnest, sparing no least effort; was he not close to Shun's not-thinking and not-striving? If one says his filial piety was one with Shun's, then Wang Xiang was Yao and Shun. If one says his grade was still far below and his mind's measure still not full, then it is hard to say that the Way of Yao and Shun was filial piety and fraternal duty and nothing more. The truth is that great Shun recognized his parent from the numinous clarity, while Wang Xiang recognized his parent from the outer wall. Great Shun saw Gusou as utterly divine and utterly sage, utterly benevolent and utterly kind; the mind that wanted to kill me and wanted to prevent my marrying — those were all later habit-minds, and his true mind was originally not like that. Even if one complied with his disordered commands and took a moment's pleasure, catering to his habit-mind, one would thereby cut through and sever the seed of the utterly divine, utterly sage, utterly benevolent, utterly kind true parent. How could the heart bear it? How could the nature endure it? Therefore Shun upheld it and stirred it by a hundred means, until the true parent appeared. As for Wang Xiang lying on the ice and the like, it was indeed a firm and deep heaven-given nature; yet what he followed and complied with was the parent of feeling and consciousness. It is also because Wang Xiang's own self had not reached the rank of Yu and Shun, and so what he recognized went no further than this. This is precisely the failure to understand goodness.

Understand goodness, and one completes that living, lively thing, born forth wherever it may be, with its own proper measure. Thus when the rod is small, one receives it; when the rod is great, one flees; one marries without informing one's parents, and so on. There is no fixed rule to be sought; one's own heart and spirit simply must be so before one is at ease. Being so oneself, one's service of one's parents is likewise so. Therefore it is said: In serving one's parents, one remonstrates at the subtle moment. The subtle moment is the first stirring of movement, the first appearing of what is auspicious. One's parents originally have only a single good heart, and then all belongs to what is auspicious and good. Even if there is a slight turning of the thought, this good heart is still faintly stirring, not yet willing to be exhausted to the end; and this too is a subtle moment for turning ill fortune into good. One who serves his parents must turn and circle precisely from this point. When the subtle moment has not yet stirred, stir it; when it has just stirred, receive and lead it on; when it has gone astray, draw it back. This is the task of using the heart to work upon the heart, of seeing the formless and hearing the soundless. Therefore one does not wait until the deed does not comply; when one sees that the parent's intent does not comply, the filial son has already spent his whole heart's plans. Only in this way can his heart be one with theirs, and he never once goes against them. Being thus sincere, thus compliant, one gathers here in a round whole the true source in which parent and I are joined as one root; one gathers here in a round whole the true source in which Heaven and Earth share one root and the ten thousand things share one body. What nature and destiny are not thereby made whole? What placing and nourishing are not thereby carried out? What change or constancy in the affairs of the world is not within the turning of my numinous clarity? This is called gathering a hundred compliances to present to one's parents. This is why great Shun's virtue made him a sage and brought him honor and support in full measure. This too is why Wu and the Duke of Zhou served the dead as the living and the departed as the present. This is what is constantly present, constantly alive, piercing the layered origins and running through the sentient and the insensate. Therefore Shun matched the mandate of Heaven and congealed the blessing of Heaven: he served his parents with Heaven. Wu sacrificed to his forebears and reached through to the suburban and ancestral temples: he served Heaven with his parents. In the end it is the one word life. Since the first coming of Heaven and Earth, there has been no day without birth; parent and I are one continuous birth, birth upon birth. Complete this life, and then all the living things of a whole age are touched and stirred by one another; only then is one said not to disgrace what gave one birth. Zhang Zai's Western Inscription is entirely an exposition of this meaning. As for Wang Xiang's filial piety, it cannot escape being a dead method. He had reached not-thinking and not-striving; yet one cannot say of him that he attained without thinking and hit the mark without striving. What are attaining and hitting the mark? They are that naturally living and lively thing which holds the formless compass and square and can complete the round and square of the whole world. Therefore it is said: The compass and square are the utmost of the round and the square; the sage is the utmost of human relations. To accord with the Way without effort is the sage. Yet if one does not attain and does not hit the mark, then it must be called thinking and striving. Thinking and striving belong to intent and consciousness; if the true nature is not brought out wholly on the platter, one leans on consciousness to do the work. But if one stirs the truth of the nature, then even such extremity of hardship and striving as Shun's wailing and lamenting and longing and complaining, when he deemed himself unfit to be a man and unfit to be a son — even so, it is still not-thinking and not-striving. Since we cannot be whole and complete from birth as Yao and Shun were, we should consider what it is that our parents gave us. It is originally not the empty skull that sees with eyes and hears with ears, not the stinking thing that is a wine sack and a rice bag. How can one bear to stop it up with muddleheadedness and pass one's days, and with this serve one's parents? Think of this, and one leaps up with a bound, the whole body breaking into sweat, and one will not consent to let the first rank under Heaven be granted to someone else. Doing one portion oneself is fulfilling filial piety and fraternal duty by one portion. When it is wholly complete, with virtue cultivated and blessing in full measure, then the filial piety of Shun and Wu as rulers, the filial piety of the Duke of Zhou as minister, and the filial piety of Confucius as uncrowned king all arrive by different roads at the same end.

He also says: Where under Heaven is there a man without filial piety? Even the unfilial man is pleased when called filial, and angry and ashamed when called unfilial. And before others he prizes reputation and puts on a show of integrity, not daring to be as unrestrained as he is in private. This too is a place where his good knowing is not drowned. Filling out this good knowing is the root of great filial piety. It is only that habit-mind and habit-energy cannot transform themselves, and so he remains unfilial as before. Analyze this clearly, and then fathers know how to teach their sons and sons know how to subdue themselves. It is like attacking a bandit: when you know where the bandit is, the day of his pacification can be predicted.

He also says: The ways in which small unfiliality is made habitual are four. The first is being pampered and doted on. Because the parents pity him overmuch, they always humor his temper; let them thwart him suddenly and he cannot bear it. They always let him have his way and let him idle at ease; let them require him to take up labor and provide support, and he is unaccustomed to it. Before others, if the child says something slightly amiss, the father cannot bear to rebuff his son; yet the son dares to rebuff his father. In letters and accomplishments, the father praises the son, only fearing that he is not above himself; but the son insists that the father should be beneath him. Having accumulated such arrogance and indulgence, in the presence of others he cannot stretch out his hand, but with his parents he can stretch it out; and so he truly believes that old and accomplished men know nothing. The second is habituation. Coarse and careless speech grows habitual, and so he dares to quarrel; casual and easy manners grow habitual, and so he dares to be unrestrained; the parents' sharing of sweets and cutting back on their own portions grows habitual, so that he no longer remembers the delicacies; the parents' bearing illness and hardship grows habitual, so that he no longer asks after their pain and care. The third is delight in self-indulgence. Seeing his peers, he cannot overcome his own temper; toward his two aged parents his taste grows thin. Entering his private quarters he shows every kind of charming manner; ascending the high hall his spirit feels stifled. He may even openly treat father and son, elder and younger brother, as vulgar creatures with whom he takes no pleasure in meeting. How then could any thought of filial piety or fraternal duty arise from within him? The fourth is forgetting kindness and remembering grievances. Kindness, when practiced long, is increasingly forgotten; grievances, when practiced long, increasingly accumulate — this is the way of human feeling. Thus a single meal produces gratitude, but when it becomes habitual the satisfaction turns to resentment; a single act of generosity produces thankfulness, but when the help is constant the question of more or less arises; a single meeting produces affection, but after many days suspicion and dislike grow heavy. How much more so with parents and brothers: one has lived with them from birth, taking their love as a fixed constant — and there are even those who, because their parents worry about them, feel offended. One takes their instruction as grating on the ear — and there are even those who, because their parents praise them, feel annoyed. One takes their labor and protection, their utmost care and management, as a matter of equality — and there are even those who, because their parents meddle in their affairs, grow angry and sullen. The great kindness before one's eyes one calmly fails to recognize — how much less can one extend it to the toil of bearing and nourishing one in the womb, the bitterness of nursing and feeding, the pain of a frail body and frightened soul? Thus there is nothing in human feeling more upside-down, more perverse, and more unnoticed by the one himself than this: a son's treatment of his parents. Rare indeed is the one who does not repay kindness with resentment. These several things are all the habitual feelings of people, yet true nature is never entirely absent; it is only that, having accumulated over long time, one does not know his own error. Therefore one should urgently wake up, early subdue and govern himself, and constantly reflect. Do not say that your parents' hearts are kind, and so you may excuse yourself; do not say that the ways of the world are thin, and so you are still better than others. The gradual accumulation of small unfilial acts becomes great unfiliality. Should one not fear?

He also says: The ways in which great unfiliality is made habitual are four. The first is private wealth. When wealth comes into my hands it becomes mine; and what is in my parents' hands I likewise think I ought to have. When wealth is sufficient one forgets one's parents; when wealth is scarce one covets what they have; when one seeks wealth and does not get it, one resents one's parents; when one's parents can no longer support themselves and must take their meals from my wealth, then one resents them again. There are even cases of a single father and an only son who come to blows over money; and of brothers, young and old, who push the burden back and forth and abandon their parents unsupported. They do not consider whose body this body is, or whose wealth this wealth is. I brought no single coin with me, yet I was nursed and fed without want, right up to today — who did that? And yet, having merely amassed a few coins, one wants to settle accounts with one's parents. The second is being attached to wife and children. Wife and children are familiar and intimate, while parents are stern and grave. When there are fine things to eat and money to spend, one wants to delight one's wife and pamper one's children; when there is a fine gathering and a good day, one wants to hold one's wife and embrace one's children — and so the thought of pleasing one's parents dwindles. One does not reflect: this child is my child, but whose child am I? If my own child belongs to me and I do not care for my parents, then what good is a child to me? That husband and wife live in harmony is indeed a joy of the household; but when one was wailing for milk, unable to tell wet from dry, what did one know of clinging to a wife? Could a wife have nursed one and brought one up? When parents see their son grown to manhood and established with a household, their joy lasts a lifetime — and now that he has a wife, are the parents to have no son at all? The third is whoring and dissipation. The fire of desire blazes, and a stranger's enticement drives one mad, so that one does not understand the grief of those who keep vigil in mourning huts. The family estate is squandered, mother-in-law and daughter-in-law quarrel, and though there are those who reproach and shame one, one does not distinguish them. One's wife carries a child and cannot sleep, while wind and rain chill the soul through the long night; one's white-haired parents have no joy, and bean broth grows cold through half a lifetime of care. Alas! How long can mad passion last? How can one bear to bring this about? The fourth is rivalry and jealousy. The world is vast, and men still feel resentment; how could parents' affection for their many children never lean to one side? So one rolls up one's sleeves and fights over shares, glares sideways to seize favor — or brothers grow sullen and unequal, or sisters reckon up the smallest fractions. Each shields his own faults and contends for superiority, splitting into factions and attacking those who differ. Slander and backbiting divide the household, and accumulated anger and favoritism thin the feeling of filial piety. These four too are the common feelings of people; it is to be feared that even a filial son may not escape them, and their course may end in great unfiliality. Ah, how alarming!

He also says: There are those who resemble the filial but are not filial. When a father has faults, one should remonstrate at the subtle moment; when he has transgressions, one should cover them over. But if one only knows how to comply with one's parents in feeling and does not know how to comply with them in principle — if one indulges their narrow prejudice and so brings discord to the whole household, or follows their willfulness and so draws hatred from the neighborhood, or shields their secret wrongdoing and so incurs guilt before Heaven and Earth — such a one compounds his parents' evil. How can that be called filial? There are those who call themselves filial and are in truth not filial: they can bear toil, they can provide support, but they wear a look of virtue. In humble households, with only this one room and father and son together morning and evening, even if words wound, the hurt soon dissolves, and instead they get frankness and full feeling. But among educated men who know letters, a son may dislike his father for being old and so call it retirement to set him aside; or dread his being stale and so find an excuse to keep away from him; or look down on him as lowly and so use reason to overawe him — until day by day they grow distant and estranged, with little to say to each other, their looks and manner cold, honoring him but not loving him. There is another sort, fond of travel, who forsakes the joy of the hall of his parents to make merry with friends, going to distant provinces and far counties, month upon month and year upon year, coveting the rich fare of others, calling it for poverty, for support, when in truth they are raising children and serving a wife. How can that be filial? And there are those who appear filial to men but are not filial in the eyes of the spirits: in life they provide support and give joy, yet their provisions are plentiful and their feeling scant, with no true gladness at all; when the parent dies, the shroud and coffin are of the finest and the wailing follows custom, yet there is no true grief; when it comes to finding a burial site, they exhaust their strength and spend their wealth — and all for the sake of seeking blessing for their sons and grandsons, not for the sake of their parents' peace. This the eyes of the spirits see most clearly. And there are those who are praised as filial for a time but cannot be so for a thousand ages; or who can be so for a thousand ages but cannot fill a single heart. Such a one offends in none of the faults above and omits nothing in the practices of filial piety, and yet has never heard the great Way; in the work of cultivating the self and fulfilling nature there are still defects, and so he remains one who falls away and loses the body, unable to repay his parents' kindness. Therefore only when virtue makes one a sage is filial piety called great. As a son, one should urgently examine himself.

He also says: The ways in which the aged become tiresome to their children and grandchildren are likewise several. The first is being old-fashioned. Their clothing, caps, and ceremonial observances no longer suit the times; but one should consider how it is that white hair comes to remain, and that there is an antique charm in it that makes people cherish them. The second is being tight-fisted with money. Scrimping and keeping accounts, they forbid their children and grandchildren to spend freely; but one should consider for whom they endured hardship, and who it was that set aside what one eats and uses each day. The third is being frail and weak. They cannot rise and sit with ease, and are hard to assist; but one should consider that to repay their toil, and to raise children against one's old age, is exactly this moment. The fourth is being muddled with age. Their speech rambles on, their hearing is dulled and their tongue halting; but one should consider that at one's own birth one knew nothing and said nothing, and who then played with one and made one laugh. The fifth is doting affection. They favor the younger children of the household, passing them their food and yielding them their clothes, protecting them overmuch; but one should consider that love should extend even to servants, and that one should understand their hearts — how much more so to one's own flesh and blood. If in these matters one raises a single thought of disgust, one enters unfiliality without knowing it. One should urgently turn back and reflect.

He also says: Again, there is the case between former and latter, between wife and concubine, where parents may show partiality, and the son easily develops resentment and complaint. Here one should give over one's heart to it, resolved to win their gladness and nothing less. Han Qi of the Song said: That a father is kind and a son filial is an ordinary thing not worth mentioning; only when parents are unkind and the son does not fail in filial piety is why antiquity and today call Shun great. The essential thing is that such feelings be melted away as quickly as possible; one in this position must let the dregs dissolve entirely, keeping not a trace of fiery temper, and compared with ordinary sons be more yielding in purpose and more attentive to giving joy, and doubly cautious. A parent with a kind heart will naturally turn to pity me; as for one without a kind heart, one cannot move him — how much less should one provoke him. One can only fulfill one's own duty as a son, so as not to fall into disobedience, and that is all. But if one sets one's mind on the parent being in the wrong, with fiery temper filling the breast, unable to dispel it and unable to shake it off, there will surely come a time when one cannot hold it back; the small root not removed, it comes at last to a bursting of the banks. I fear that at such a time the blame laid on the parent will be light, while the son's crime will be past escaping.
